Q: Why does asyncio.TaskGroup intermittently deadlock when combining asyncio.to_thread(), nested cancellation, and contextvars in Python 3.12? A:

Disclaimer: this is not "here, it is resolved" answer, because I could not reproduce your error to start.

For one, there were really a lot of bug-fixes in a somewhat extensive rewrite of Asyncio for Python 3.14 so that async code can take advantage of the free-threaded Python module - here is a blog post from the author for the fixes https://labs.quansight.org/blog/scaling-asyncio-on-free-threaded-python. - so if you cn update your workfow for Python 3.14 and what you've hit there is a bug related to it, it will probably just go away.

Also, I used Python 3.12.13 - if you can't change to 3.14, try at least the latest stable 3.12.

Now, going to your specific topics at the end of the question:

Can nested task cancellation combined with asyncio.to_thread() leave a TaskGroup waiting indefinitely?

Your MRE doesn't feature any "nested task"s. But regardless, if an errored task bubbles up its error up to a task spawned by the Threadgroup, that should cancel the whole group, but a cancelled task won't stop any other tasks in the group.

Are there known edge cases involving contextvars propagation across worker threads that could explain this behavior?

contextvars do not propagate values to other threads if you start them manually (create a thread instance and call thread.start(), but the asyncio mechanism behind the ".to_thread" call does so. I changed your example to actually read the contextvar value in the off-thread worker (And added some "print" calls): it also works fine in Python 3.12.13

Is this expected behavior, a misuse of TaskGroup, or a potential CPython bug?

So, you might reach cPython 3.12 bugs with asyncio and multi-threaded - if that is not the case, your example code here simply is not triggering your issue.

The only incorrect assumption I found is that once a function is called off thread with to_thread it won't really stop until it finishes: it doesn't know, and have no way to know, unless one puts calls to inspect at intervals (in the off-thread for i) to check if the parent task was cancelled in the original thread: Python has no means to send signals to code running in threads. So each off-thread worker started will run to completion.

It may be that in your real code (not this snippet) your off-thread code depends on some global resource becoming available or changing state, so they will hang.

Another thing to keep in mind is that raising asyncio.CancelledError (and therefore, canceling a task with a cancel call) won't really stop that tasks's siblings to end: all others will run to completion inside a taskgroup. But if one of the tasks raises anotehr error than CancelledError, then, yes, all sibling tasks are cancelled! (they get an exception thrown at the await asyncio.to_thread and finish from there - but any work already started off-thread is carried to completion, as stated above).

I have instrumented your same snippet with prints and a parallel count of off-thread workers, so it is possible to check the sync across the contextvar and the actual running code. You can change the error thrown from CancelledError to RuntimeError to see the behavior change in the TaskGroup -

import asyncio
import contextvars
import random
import threading

import time

request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id")

async def worker(i):
    print(f"task {i} starting")
    request_id.set(i)

    done = False
    try:
        await asyncio.to_thread(cpu_work)
        done = True
        await asyncio.sleep(random.random() /100) # + 1.1)  # random() /100 would often just fall bellow the minimum task switch threshold of 5ms
        print(f"task {i} resuming")
    finally:
        if done:
            async_work_incomplete.remove(i)
    if random.randint(0, 5) == 0:
        print(f"cancelling everything from {i}")
        raise asyncio.CancelledError()
        raise RuntimeError()

worker_counter = 1
async_work_incomplete = set()
off_thread_work_incomplete = set()
lock = threading.Lock()



def cpu_work():
    global worker_counter
    with lock:
        id = worker_counter
        worker_counter +=1
    off_thread_work_incomplete.add(id)
    total = 0
    try:
        print(f"starging worker {id}, contextvar: {request_id.get("X")}")

        for i in range(15_000_000):
            total += i
        print(f"ending worker {id}")
    except BaseException as interrupt:
        print(f"****** argh! {interrupt}")
        raise


    off_thread_work_incomplete.remove(id)
    return total

async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            for i in range(1, 50):
                async_work_incomplete.add(i)

                tg.create_task(worker(i))
    finally:
        print(f"wrapping up. Unfinished tasks: {async_work_incomplete}")
        print(f"wrapping up. Unfinished off_thread workers: {off_thread_work_incomplete}")

        time.sleep(2)
        print(f"wrapping up. Unfinished off_thread workers after pause: {off_thread_work_incomplete}")

asyncio.run(main())

Q: What is the exact object construction timeline for a built-in data member initialized using a member initializer list? A:

The fact that it's as build-in type doesn't change the basics of how the initialization list works. And particularly, the fact that (as the name implies) the objects are actually initialized, not default constructed, and then assigned to.

So, in theory, the ctor with the initializer list (Account(int x) : balance(x) {}) creates balance with code that passes x to the ctor, roughly equivalent to int balance{x}.

The unusual points about a built-in type like int are that at least on most hardware, the "contructur" is almost entirely a conceptual construct (that doesn't generate any code), and there's almost no way to detect the difference between code like int x{y}; vs. int x; x = y;.

Q: How Do I Make a 3d Matrix Out Of Multiple 2d Matrices in C#? A:

You were close with your second attempt, you just had your array syntax backwards.

  • Piece[,][] (what you had) is a 2d array of arrays. So it'd be like a single board, where each space contains multiple values.
  • Piece[][,] (what you want) is an array of 2d arrays. A list of multiple boards.
Piece[][,] allBoards = [ board1, board2 ];

Q: predeclared any requires go1.18 or later (-lang was set to go1.16; check go.mod) A:

I think the diagnosis here https://github.com/golang/go/issues/76932 is correct - the go.mod in question in generated on the fly by _content/tour/static/js/services.js. That fix doesn't work for me (syntax errors in the version numbers), but this version does:

            const hasGoMod = code.includes('\n-- go.mod --\n') || code.startsWith('-- go.mod --\n');
            if (!hasGoMod) {
                code += '\n-- go.mod --' +
                    '\nmodule example' +
                    '\n' +
                    '\ngo 1.25' +
                    '\n' +
                    '\nrequire (' +
                    '\n golang.org/x/tour v0.1.0' +
                    '\n golang.org/x/crypto v0.54.0' +
                    '\n golang.org/x/net v0.57.0' +
                    '\n golang.org/x/sys v0.47.0' +
                    '\n golang.org/x/text v0.40.0' +
                    '\n golang.org/x/tools v0.48.0' +
                    '\n)'
            }

(I copied the version numbers from related go.mod files in the package and its requirements - naturally, those would need to be updated when the package changes). Also, older pages recommend go install golang.org/x/tour@latest but newer pages say go install golang.org/x/website/tour@latest is correct (and that's what worked for me).

I found it necessary to re-run the install after modifying services.js and then do a hard refresh in the browser to make sure I flushed the old version of services.js

Q: eabihf What is hf standing for? A:

"hf" stands for "hard float". More specifically eabihf means the "hard float ABI" is used. Assuming you are using a VFP FPU, "hard float ABI" refers to the "VFP and SIMD vector Register Arguments" variant defined in the arm architecture procedure call specification.

This variant, as the name suggests, normally passes floating point values in vfp registers. In principle similar variants could have been defined for other, incompatible, floating point units but to the best of my knowledge none were.

It is possible to use hardware floating point without using the "baseline" ABI but this has two downsides.

  • Extra instructions are required to shunt floating point values back and forth between vfp registers and main registers (or the stack). Depending on how exactly vfp is implemented these instructions may be relatively slow.
  • Arm only has four 32-bit main registers used for parameter passing with the result that double precision floating point values will often overflow onto the stack.

In gcc/clang, these are controlled by the -mfloat-abi command line switch.

  • -mfloat-abi=soft - software floating point
  • -mfloat-abi=softfp - hardware floating point, but still using the baseline (soft-float) ABI.
  • -mfloat-abi=hard - hardware floating point with the hard-float ABI.

IIRC The initial hard float porting was done without changing the gnu triple, but it was later decided that a separate triple made sense. Markers were also added to object files to prevent accidental linking of code using the hard-float ABI with code using the soft-float ABI.
